messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 57
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Detective
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 54

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Somatic (Breathlessness): Difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath, Olfactory (Sweat/Body): Sweat or body odour, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Face Hiding: cover face with hands, Redirection: I think of something else, Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform
  Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Memory: Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down

Vignette:
Marisol Ortega is a 57-year-old detective who came to treatment after months of telling herself that what happened was simply another hard thing to get through on the job. She had been divorced for years and was used to relying on herself. In police work, that self-reliance had become part of her identity. The incident she returns to happened during what was first described over the radio as a routine welfare check at a small industrial property on the edge of the city. By the time Marisol and the other responders entered the building, there was already a sharp, sterile chemical smell in the air, mixed with the heavy smell of sweat from people moving quickly in protective gear and from workers who had stumbled outside in distress. Someone was coughing. Someone else shouted for medical support. Marisol remembers her own breathing changing first into shallow pulls and then into a frightening sense that no breath was enough. She recalls the sound of sudden yelling and equipment clattering, but when she tries to tell it in order, the scene breaks apart. There is the antiseptic smell, a flash of bright light on concrete, the pressure in her chest, her hand going to her face, and then a sense of the whole thing rushing at her as if it is still underway.

Afterward, her memories never settled into a single narrative. She described them as pieces that do not connect properly. If she gets close to the moment when she could no longer breathe comfortably, her mind veers away and she pushes the rest out before it can fully come back. What she does remember often does not feel like remembering. If she catches the smell of hospital disinfectant in an elevator, or antiseptic wipes at a clinic, she is no longer simply a detective in the present day; for a few moments it feels to her as if she is back in that building, chest tight, trying to orient herself while everyone is shouting. The smell of body odour or sweat on a crowded train platform can do something similar, especially in close spaces where the air feels used up. More than once she has stepped off suddenly, covering her face with both hands as if that might block whatever is coming toward her.

Marisol kept working, but her work began to narrow around what she felt she could manage. In the precinct she became intensely aware of every abrupt sound—the crackle of a radio at full volume, a slammed metal door, a burst of raised voices from the booking area. Her body stayed braced, shoulders high, muscles tight, as if impact were imminent. She scans every room without meaning to, checking exits, ventilation, who is nearby, what they are wearing, whether anything seems off. She knows this is exhausting, but she has come to believe she has to be on guard all the time. To let down for even a minute feels unsafe.

She also found herself reacting strongly to authority and uniformed personnel in ways that embarrassed her. At interagency meetings, especially when command staff or officials from outside departments were present, she stayed to the edges or invented reasons not to attend. She did not explain that what was hardest was being around the people she felt should have protected her and did not. In her view, the institutions in charge failed at the most basic level. The site should have been safer, the response clearer, the risks communicated better. Being near uniforms now carries not reassurance but a hard, private anger and mistrust. She says very little about this at work, choosing instead to think of something else, redirecting her mind to case details, paperwork, anything cleaner and more contained than the fragments that threaten to surface.

Over the past year, those habits have begun to cost her. Colleagues have noticed that she withdraws after sudden commotion and that she sometimes goes silent in briefings. A younger detective asked if she was all right after Marisol abruptly covered her face during a noisy hallway exchange and walked out. She told him it was nothing, but later sat alone in her car until her breathing slowed. Outside of work she has become more cut off. She no longer trusts her own feelings in the way she once did. What troubles her most is not only the fear that her body can turn on her without warning, but her conviction that something in her emotional life has gone flat for good. She says she cannot remember the last time she felt fully normal, fully warm, fully present with anyone.

What finally brought her in was a recent moment at the hospital, where she had gone for a non-urgent medical appointment. The antiseptic smell hit her at the entrance, followed by the sound of a cart crashing somewhere down the corridor. Instantly she was on high alert, hand over her face, chest tight, searching the hallway for danger while knowing, at some level, that there was no chemical leak there. She left before being seen. Sitting in the parking garage afterward, furious and shaken, Marisol recognized that this was no longer something she could outwork or outthink. She is seeking help now because she is afraid that if this continues, her world will keep shrinking—at work, in public, inside herself. At the same time, she is hoping, cautiously, that she might not have to feel on guard every minute of the day, and that the event might someday feel like something that happened, rather than something she is still trapped inside.
